title: Spectroscopic Signatures of Polaronic Density Wave Fluctuations in Superconducting Bismuthates
summary: The bismuthate high-temperature superconductors have been identified as potential bipolaron systems, where hole pairs are bound to local breathing distortions of the BiO$_6$ octahedra in their metallic phase. However, obtaining definitive evidence for these quasiparticles and their excitations remains challenging. Here, we report on periodic modulations of the spectral intensities and scattering rates of quasiparticles on the Fermi surfaces of doped bismuthates Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$BiO$_3$ and BaPb$_{1-y}$Bi$_y$O$_3$, which are reminiscent of ``hot spot'' patterns that have been observed in cuprate superconductors. We show that these features can be well described by a model where electrons couple to fluctuating density wave modulations with short-range coherence along a $(\pi,\pi,\pi)$-oriented wavevector. The results are consistent with the existence of a two-component fluid where unpaired electrons interact with a fluctuating density wave created by residual bipolarons and their breathing distortions of the BiO$_6$ octahedra.

title: Crystal-Symmetry-Dependent Field-Free Superconducting Diode Effect in CoPt/Nb Heterostructures
summary: Superconducting diodes convert nonreciprocal critical currents into current-polarity-selective switching between zero-resistance and resistive states. However, realizing the superconducting diode effect often requires complex device architectures and an external magnetic field to break spatial-inversion and time-reversal symmetry, substantially limiting its integration into cryogenic electronics and superconducting quantum circuits. Here, we demonstrate precise control of the field-free superconducting diode effect in epitaxial [111]-oriented A1-CoPt/Nb heterostructures. The critical-current asymmetry obeys the magnetic-point-group symmetry relation: it is finite along low-symmetry directions, suppressed along magnetic mirror axes, and reverses under either a 60{\deg} in-plane rotation or reversal of the CoPt magnetization. The same threefold symmetry dependence is observed in field-free current-induced magnetization switching in A1-CoPt films, indicating a common crystallographic origin for the superconducting and normal-state transport responses. Current- and temperature-dependent second-harmonic transport measurements are consistent with vortex-mediated nonreciprocity arising from an orientation-dependent interfacial edge landscape. We further exploit the magnetization-dependent diode polarity for proof-of-concept superconducting readout of electrically written magnetic states. These results establish crystallographic symmetry as an effective degree of freedom for engineering the superconducting diode effect, expanding the accessible materials space and providing a practical route toward field-free superconducting electronics.

title: Superconductivity from the Berry connection from many-electron wave functions: $U(1)$ gauge fluctuation, gauge invariance, and superconductivity
summary: The electromagnetic $U(1)$ gauge invariance and superconductivity are examined by employing the Berry connection from many-electron wave functions and the fluctuations of it that give rise to the probabilistic random transitions among quantum states. The gauge invariance in the classical electrodynamics is regarded as the requirement that extracts unaffected parts by the gauge fluctuation. In quantum mechanics, dissipation-free states from the gauge fluctuation exist, and we identify them as superconducting states. We explain the reversible superconducting-normal phase transition in a magnetic field including the force balance. The present superconductivity theory lifts two fundamental disagreements between theory and experiment existing in the current standard theory with keeping the major results by the BCS theory. Thus, it may be considered as a superconductivity theory encompassing the current standard one.

title: Superconductivity from a Cooper surface instability in a nodal Bose metal
summary: In underdoped cuprates, the superconducting gap is largest where low-energy electron spectral weight is already depleted above the transition. How can a weak attraction drive superconductivity when the one-electron density of states vanishes? In a momentum-space \(t\)--\(J\) model, the exactly solvable normal state is a nodal Bose metal with four one-electron nodes. Along two contours called Cooper surfaces, adding or removing a spin-singlet pair of electrons with opposite momenta costs no energy. The resulting logarithmic divergence of the pair susceptibility allows an arbitrarily weak pair-transfer attraction to stabilize a correlated nodal \(d\)-wave superconductor. Spin-resolved coincidence photoemission could test this pairing mechanism by resolving two zero-energy pair-removal ridges above the transition and a third along the underlying Luttinger surface below it.

title: Dressed Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory: Opening and Closing a Pandora's box
summary: Dressed time-dependent density functional theory (DTDDFT) has been shown to overcome the inability of adiabatic TDDFT to describe excitation energies and oscillator strengths of double-excitation character, however, it is far from being a black-box method. Here, we outline and address several operational issues while benchmarking the approach on a range of molecules. We define a protocol to determine whether an excitation from adiabatic TDDFT needs a double-excitation correction, without requiring a priori knowledge of the state, and which Kohn-Sham states to build the frequency-dependent DTDDFT matrix from. We present an 'undownfolding' that replaces this frequency-dependent matrix by a linear frequency-independent one in a larger space, eliminating ambiguities in the iterative procedure required to diagonalize the former. We compare the performance of DTDDFT for both excitation energies and oscillator strengths, as measured by an approximate metric for their single-excitation character, for different choices of the underlying adiabatic density functional approximation, with and without employing the Tamm-Dancoff approximation, for molecular excitations predicted by wavefunction methods to have either partial or genuine double-excitation character. We propose a correction to DTDDFT to account for missing dynamical correlation that is removed in the truncation procedure inherent in the method, and discuss the possibility of unphysical imaginary frequencies reminiscent of the 'triplet instability' that may arise. We provide benchmark data for butadiene, hexatriene, octatetraene, cyclopentadiene, acrolein, naphthalene, ethylene, borole, and cyclopentadienone. In some cases, DTDDFT predicts frequencies with about as much accuracy as the same underlying adiabatic TDDFT predicts for the constituent and near-lying single excitations.

title: Computing hydration free energies and crystalline solubility of drug-like molecules with MACE
summary: Accurate prediction of thermodynamic solubility is critical in drug discovery, where it influences oral bioavailability and drives decisions in formulation chemistry. First-principles calculations of intrinsic solubility offer the potential to achieve superior generalization to existing direct, data-driven predictors, which often suffer significant performance degradation outside of their training distribution. Whilst free energy perturbation calculations provide a rigorous framework to estimate these quantities, their accuracy is typically limited by the quality of the empirical force field used. In this work, we present a computational workflow driven by the MACE family of machine learning interatomic potentials to compute the solubility of neutral drug-like molecules. We introduce $\lambda$-MACE, a potential optimised for condensed-phase free energy calculations, which enables hydration free energy calculations at experimental accuracy on an evaluation set of 70 compounds from the FreeSolv database selected for their relevance to medicinal chemistry. We further combine these hydration free energy calculations with sublimation free energy calculations to predict crystalline solubility given a known experimental crystal structure, on an additional set of 10 compounds. We achieve state-of-the-art performance for each leg of the calculation, with experimental accuracy for the hydration leg, and accuracy competitive with industry-standard DFT for the sublimation leg. However, the overall errors after combining both legs lead to accuracy of 1.53 log units. This is significantly above the experimental accuracy (0.17-0.6 log units). Closing this gap will require substantially tighter accuracy in each leg, on the order of half of chemical accuracy (0.5 kcal/mol), with crystalline thermodynamics the hardest remaining challenge.

title: Analytic sc$GW$ nuclear gradients with the resolution-of-identity approximation
summary: We present the first fully analytic derivation and implementation of nuclear gradients for the finite-temperature sc$GW$ method. The derivation is formulated within the $\Phi$-derivable framework of sc$GW$, using a Lagrangian formulation to obtain the analytic gradients. With the resolution-of-identity approximation, the computational cost of evaluating the gradients scales as $O(N_{\tau}N_\text{aux}^{2}N_\text{AO}^{2})$, exhibiting the same asymptotic scaling as the parent sc$GW$ method. Using the newly implemented analytic gradients, we perform geometry optimizations for several molecular systems and benchmark the resulting structures against those obtained with Hartree--Fock, $G_{0}W_{0}$, MP2, CCSD, and CCSD(T). We find that sc$GW$ generally yields reasonable molecular geometries, with its performance being comparable to that of CCSD for several systems. Overall, these results demonstrate the potential of analytic sc$GW$ gradients for reliable geometry optimizations for molecular systems while retaining the favorable $O(N_{\tau}N_\text{aux}^{2}N_\text{AO}^2)$ scaling of the underlying method.

title: OrbACE: Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion
summary:
Accurate electronic-structure reference data are expensive, motivating interatomic potentials that learn effectively from limited training sets. We introduce OrbACE (Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion), a framework that supplements an E(3)-equivariant cluster-expansion backbone with inexpensive electronic-structure descriptors. On ANI-1x at the $\omega$B97X/6-31G* level, its atom-centered variant, OrbACE-A, trained on 10,000 configurations and evaluated on 442,000 held-out configurations, achieves energy and force mean absolute errors of 3.16 meV/atom and 76 meV/angstrom in direct learning, compared with 9.61 meV/atom and 146 meV/angstrom for MACE with matched backbone settings. This reduces the energy error by a factor of three and approximately halves the force error. Its energy error is also below that of the best delta-corrected MACE baseline, 5.00 meV/atom, although its force error is slightly higher. Combining OrbACE-A with a Hartree-Fock delta baseline further reduces the errors to 1.48 meV/atom and 35 meV/angstrom.
  OrbACE-A builds atom- and pair-resolved invariants from a non-self-consistent extended-Hueckel model evaluated within the differentiable forward pass, yielding forces consistent with the predicted energy. The orbital variant, OrbACE-O, instead uses localized Hartree-Fock orbitals as graph nodes, with scalar and equivariant electronic descriptors. Its forces are evaluated at fixed descriptors, omitting their response to nuclear motion. In direct learning on ANI-1x, its energy error is approximately three times that of OrbACE-A. The three benchmarks considered (ANI-1x, revised MD17, and 3BPA) cover neutral, closed-shell, non-periodic molecules containing H, C, N, and O. Performance outside this domain remains to be established.

title: TyxonQ: A Workflow Layer for Quantum Computing in Chemistry
summary:
Quantum computational chemistry is often framed around a hybrid quantum solver. In practical applications, however, bottlenecks to adoption also lie in the surrounding multiscale workflow. A molecular problem may combine classical molecular mechanics and dynamics, conventional electronic-structure calculations, and a quantum solver for selected orbitals or embedded fragments. This division of work is particularly relevant when a chemically important electronic subspace is strongly correlated. The size of the electronic Hilbert space and the qubit, noise, and circuit-depth constraints of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices make active-space and embedding choices central to a feasible quantum calculation. The resulting energies and gradients must remain consistent with the surrounding classical simulation.
  We present TyxonQ, a workflow layer that connects these levels of treatment rather than addressing only the hybrid quantum algorithm. Four integration interfaces link PySCF-compatible energy/force scanners and embedding, solver adapters, simulator and hardware backends, and classical consumers. The implementation combines QM/MM and fragment embedding with conventional CCSD/FCI fragment solvers, variational and sampling-based quantum methods, and adapters for ASE, i-PI, OpenMM, LAMMPS (through i-PI), and MDI. We describe the contracts and audit coverage, and evaluate correctness, switching cost, reproducibility, and artifact portability on small chemistry workflows, distinguishing executed paths from source-level support. The purpose of TyxonQ is to support incremental integration of quantum calculations into existing computational chemistry workflows, including those used in industry, while retaining appropriate classical treatments elsewhere.

title: Bringing Singles to $GW$: A Coupled-Cluster Perspective on Orbital Relaxation
summary: The one-shot $G_0W_0$ approximation suffers from a pronounced dependence on the underlying mean-field starting point. Here, we explore an alternative to conventional self-consistent $GW$ schemes by introducing single excitations within the recently established connection between $GW$ and extended coupled-cluster (ECC) theory. Starting from the equivalence between $G_0W_0$ and ionization-potential/electron-affinity equation-of-motion direct-ring extended coupled-cluster doubles (IP/EA-EOM-drECCD), we extend the formalism to include right-hand single-excitation and left-hand single-deexcitation cluster amplitudes coupled to the direct-ring doubles amplitudes. The resulting approximation, denoted singles-$G_0W_0$ (s$G_0W_0$), incorporates orbital-relaxation effects without explicitly introducing self-consistency in the Green's function. We assess the performance of s$G_0W_0$ for molecular valence and core ionization potentials using Hartree-Fock and Kohn-Sham starting points. For both types of ionizations, the inclusion of singles largely suppresses the starting-point dependence observed in conventional $G_0W_0$, yielding quasiparticle energies close to those obtained from the Hartree-Fock reference, irrespective of the initial mean-field description. Although this does not necessarily translate into improved absolute accuracy, it demonstrates that singles provide an effective route to reducing the starting-point dependence of $GW$-like approximations without resorting to self-consistency.

title: PineIR: 3D molecular structures from an infrared spectrum alone
summary: Computing the infrared (IR) spectrum of a molecule from its structure is routine. The inverse problem is not. In practice, IR spectra are used to identify the functional groups present in a molecule, while the determination of its complete structure requires additional measurements. Machine-learning models that return 3D structures from IR spectra exist, but all of them need extra input, such as Raman, ultraviolet or nuclear magnetic resonance spectra, the molecular formula, or the number of atoms. In this work we present PineIR, a generative model that returns 3D molecular structures from the IR spectrum alone. PineIR builds the molecule atom by atom, and each atom is associated with its contribution to the IR spectrum. This contribution is subtracted from the input spectrum before the next atom is generated. To train it, we computed with a machine-learned interatomic potential the IR spectra of 4.6 million structures of 3.1 million molecules, including conformer ensembles. On computed spectra of held-out molecules, the best-ranked of fifty candidates has the correct connectivity in 43% of the cases, and the generated geometries reproduce the conformer and the diastereomer that produced the input spectrum. After fine-tuning on 161k spectra calculated with the hybrid functional B3LYP, the model can also be applied to spectra at this level of theory.

title: Automatic dual basis sets for self-consistent field calculations
summary: Density functional theory (DFT) has long been the workhorse of electronic structure theory, and it is experiencing a new boom thanks to big data applications and machine learning. A DFT calculation requires the iterative solution of the self-consistent field (SCF) problem, whose cost is the product of (i) the number of SCF steps and (ii) the cost of a single step. The number of SCF steps depends strongly on the initial guess, regardless of the SCF algorithm, and quantitative DFT accuracy is known to require at least a polarized triple-$\zeta$ basis set. However, a qualitatively correct solution may often be found already in a smaller \emph{dual basis} (DB), which can then bootstrap a calculation in the full basis set. Traditionally, the DB is chosen by hand for each application to enable robust convergence to the ground state. In this work, we pursue automatic generation of DBs for SCF calculations. Our generator constructs a pruned orbital basis from the target orbital basis for a predefined precision threshold and a given Fock matrix. As expected, the larger the basis set is, the smaller the fraction of kept basis functions. The DBs produced by our algorithm exhibit similar performance for a wide range of systems from the first 4 periods of the periodic table. Ultimately, we find that presently available initial guesses for the Fock matrix are not accurate enough to unlock the use of adaptive basis sets, and believe that the same limitation may hold for similar attempts for basis compactification.

title: A general-purpose electron density model for molecular chemistry
summary: Universal machine-learning potentials predict molecular structure and stability at the accuracy of quantum mechanics, for a fraction of the cost. Properties derived instead from knowledge of the electronic structure give profound insights into chemical reactivity, but are not accessible with the same ease or transferability. We train PET-rho-OMol25, a model of the ground-state electron density and spin polarization of molecular systems on four million OMol25 structures in multiple charge and spin states. The model makes predictions for entire proteins in a few seconds on a single GPU, and enables estimation of important diagnostics of molecular structure and reactivity, such as vibrational Stark measurements, halogen $\sigma$-holes, hydrogen-bond basicities and core-level shifts, as well as spin density for redox chemistry and magnetism. PET-rho-OMol25 has an accuracy close to density-functional theory, with its least reliable predictions flagged by its built-in uncertainty estimator, for most properties and classes of compounds. It can be used as a drop-in replacement for electronic-structure calculations of the density, making insightful analyses available for larger and more complex structures.

title: A nonequilibrium-capturing unified gas-kinetic scheme II: multi-frequency radiation transport
summary: Conventional discrete ordinate methods are widely used for thermal radiative transfer, but their fixed number of angular degrees of freedom (DoFs) incurs unnecessary computational cost near equilibrium. We therefore develop a nonequilibrium-capturing unified gas-kinetic scheme (NCUGKS) for multi-frequency radiation transport. The scheme preserves the mul tiscale capability of UGKS through interface evolution that couples transport and collision. Radiation intensity is expanded in an orthonormal basis of the discrete angular space. The expansion coefficients serve as angular DoFs, with their number adapted independently to local nonequilibrium in each cell, frequency group, and quadrant. At each time step, the coefficients to be evolved are selected using the exponentially decayed contribution from the previous step and the requirements of interface transport. The selected coefficients are advanced by the finite volume scheme and corrected to match the macroscopic radiation energy before higher-degree coefficients are discarded according to the prescribed relative tail tolerance. Therefore, in the optically thick limit, the resulting representation retains only one angular DoF per quadrant. Numerical tests spanning different optical regimes show close agreement with reference solutions, validating its accuracy. Furthermore, in terms of memory and computational efficiency, the proposed method reduces memory by factors from 21.7 to 154.0 and achieves speedups from 24.87 to 257.9 compared with the original discrete ordinate UGKS. NCUGKS thus provides the ability to accurately simulate multiscale ra diative transfer with reduced memory and computational costs. The proposed approach also offers a framework for adapting angular degrees of freedom in other discrete ordinate methods.

title: Estimating subcritical multiplication from stochastic neutron noise: a branching Brownian motion model for leakage counts
summary: A neutron detector placed outside a subcritical system records fission chains as correlated bursts of counts. The time dependence of these correlations gives access to the $\alpha$ eigenvalues governing the decay of the system and, with additional physical information, to its effective multiplication factor $k_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The usual analysis relies on point kinetics, which ignores where chains are born and which neutrons escape. We examine this approximation in a model simple enough to be solved: branching Brownian motion, that is, one-group neutron diffusion with capture and fission, in a domain whose absorbing boundary plays the role of the detector. For a stationary Poisson source we derive the Feynman $Y$ function (the count variance-to-mean ratio minus one) by following pairs of neutrons from their common ancestor to their detection. In a homogeneous cube the result is an explicit sum over spatial modes whose weights are fixed by the geometry and the source. We compare it with direct branching simulations and with one-speed OpenMC transport calculations in which fission is sampled with analog reaction selection and FREYA multiplicities. At the longest simulated gate the model agrees with transport to about $1\%$ at $k=0.8$ and $0.9$, and to $10\%$ at $k=0.5$. The corresponding point-model discrepancies range from $25$ to $48\%$. When geometry, source and material parameters are known, retaining the spatial modes also reduces the bias on the inferred multiplication factor. Two extensions prepare the use of the model in inverse problems. Correlations between opposite faces distinguish systems that share the same fundamental decay rate but differ in leakage, and a hierarchy of three stationary problems links this spatial benchmark to multiplicity counting. Modal convergence, detector imbalance and spectral evolution remain limitations for quantitative inference.

title: AI Buckingham: Agentic Discovery of Dimensionless Scaling Laws Across Physical Regimes
summary: Classical dimensional analysis defines admissible dimensionless representations but does not determine which combinations capture the dominant physical dependence, whether it changes across physical regimes, or when dependent-variable rescaling is required. We present AI Buckingham, an agentic framework for autonomous dimensionless discovery from natural-language descriptions of physical problems and observational data. It couples reasoning and planning by a large language model (LLM) with predefined symbolic and numerical tools. Literature-based knowledge retrieval supports dimensional checking, gradient-based clustering identifies physical regimes, and mutual information provides an objective, reparameterization-invariant criterion for identifying dominant dimensionless groups. Explicit numerical criteria determine the group count and assess simplification. Across ten physical systems spanning fluid dynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, thermal convection and additive manufacturing, AI Buckingham recovers established similarity representations and resolves regime-dependent scalings. For the longstanding challenge of predicting turbulent drag on rough surfaces, it identifies informative reparameterizations of surface statistics that improve equivalent sand-grain roughness estimates for engineering-oriented drag modelling.

title: Numerical model for ice formation in soil samples
summary:
Ice formation, or in general liquid crystallization, in porous media is important in various engineering contexts ranging
  from frost heave in soils to structural damage due to salt crystallization. Developing mesoscopic models for this problem is challenging due to the multitude of phenomena involved - fluid flow, phase transitions and complex porous geometries. In this work, we present an efficient numerical implementation addressing this class of problems. We use a phase field model with a non-conserved order parameter for liquid crystallization and solve it in a Lattice-Boltzmann framework. Our modifications to the phase field model enable the direct capture of important thermodynamic phenomena such as the Gibbs-Thomson effect and Soil Freezing Characteristic Curve (SFCC). We demonstrate our model's capabilities in sphere packings as well as in realistic soil geometries. Our model is able to resolve the pore-scale freezing and capture the macroscopic freezing behavior such as the hysteresis observed during freezing and thawing.

title: StePPO: Adaptive Step-Size Control for Initial-Value Problems Using Proximal Policy Optimisation
summary: ODE solvers are used to model, simulate, and analyse continuous-time systems found in many signal processing applications. Time integration of these initial-value problems is traditionally performed using adaptive embedded Runge--Kutta methods. For proper time-step selection, adaptive solvers accept or reject each candidate step according to a local error estimate. Their efficiency is therefore controlled by the rule that selects the next step size. Classical proportional--integral--derivative (PID) controllers are computationally inexpensive per decision and reliable, but their reactive design can lead to costly numerical solves near stiff transitions. We formulate step-size selection for parametrised IVPs as a Markov decision process and train a continuous-action policy using proximal policy optimisation. The policy processes its observation signals using a deep network while maintaining the embedded solver logic. We evaluate on a decay function, the Van der Pol system, and the Brusselator system at matched tolerances, and compare against a standard PID controller and a multi-scale DeepONet network. We find that the proposed learned policy remains within prescribed error tolerances while reducing the required number of solve steps by up to 60%, achieving a wall-clock time reduction of 58%, for both in- and out-of-distribution settings.

title: A Monolithic Fully Eulerian Lattice Boltzmann Framework for Fluid--Structure Interaction with Neo-Hookean Elastic Solids
summary: We present a fully Eulerian, monolithic lattice Boltzmann method for fluid--structure interaction with incompressible neo-Hookean solids at unequal densities, and use it to compute the Turek--Hron FSI2 and FSI3 benchmarks on a single Cartesian grid. A pressure-based kinetic scheme advances the mixture momentum, a polynomial MTHINC reconstruction transports the solid volume fraction with closed-form fluxes, and the left Cauchy--Green tensor gives the elastic stress; all updates are explicit and local. Because the density is transported independently of the populations, two corrections are introduced. A lattice-link correction makes uniform translation an exact discrete solution for any density ratio, which is verified to round-off up to $\rho_s/\rho_f=1000$. A pressure-mode correction, derived from an asymptotic analysis of the scheme, removes the frame-dependent defect that otherwise causes a secular drift of the solid mass. The verification separates the two sources of error: the scheme is second-order accurate towards the diffuse-interface solution at fixed interface thickness, and first-order towards the sharp-interface solution when the thickness scales with the grid, as predicted by an estimate of the interfacial truncation error. The method reproduces a deformable disk in Taylor--Green and lid-driven-cavity flows, and the FSI3 and FSI2 benchmarks at density ratios of one and ten.
